title: Anyone use AI to help visualise rigging on non humanoids?
author: AethericPulse

comments.author: GigaTerra
comments.body:
Interesting and useful, but it is showing a shortcoming, since it is trained on the most commonly available data it doesn't know about advance rigging tricks. For example the joints here would fold unrealistically because real bone joints deform in a curve, not around an axis. Tricks like double knee joints, or inverse bones, extended bones and 3rd knee bones. These are all tricks invented to fix the issues caused by this type of rigging. 

AI works with the most common knowledge, making the most common mistakes. Not that this is bad, but an library of professional data should be build to make professional quality AI.

replies.author: AethericPulse
replies.body:
I was working on the rig already with Claude and wanted a visual on how the upper leg connects to the hip and how the jaw should connect because the initial rig by Claude wasn't right so I asked it to research it further highlighting my concerns and produce a prompt for me, note this was a first revision as I just needed a rough idea:


Create a clear, technical anatomical diagram showing the ideal skeletal rigging for a stylized 3D boar character, suitable for use as a reference for bone placement in Blender. Style: clean illustration,

side view profile of the boar in neutral pose, bones rendered as solid octahedrons (Blender style) overlaid on a semi-transparent boar silhouette so anatomy and bones are both visible. Each bone clearly

labeled with its name and a small arrow.

The rig must support these actions:

Charge attack (forward lunge with body rotation)

Tusk gore (head swipe up/sideways)

Bite attack (mouth opens, head thrusts forward)

Idle breathing (chest expansion, subtle spine flex)

Hit reaction (whole-body flinch)

Death collapse (legs fold, body drops)


Required bones, anatomically positioned:

1. Root — world origin, base of rig


2. Hips — over rear hip joint, controls back half


3. Spine — mid-body, between hips and ribcage


4. Chest — over ribcage, controls front body


5. Neck — between shoulders and skull


6. Head — from skull base to nose tip


7. Jaw — child of Head, hinged at TMJ joint just below ear, extending forward to chin (allows mouth open/close)


8. L/R Shoulder (clavicle) — connects Chest to front leg


9. L/R Hip (pelvis) — connects Hips to back leg


10. FL/FR/BL/BR UpperLeg — femur/humerus, from shoulder/hip down to knee


11. FL/FR/BL/BR LowerLeg — tibia/radius, from knee to ankle


12. FL/FR/BL/BR Foot — hoof bone, from ankle forward into hoof tip


13. Tail_1, Tail_2, Tail_3 — three short segments for tail flick



Annotations to include in the image:

Arrow at the TMJ (jaw hinge) showing rotation axis for mouth opening

Arrow at Hips showing rotation axis for charge motion

Arrow at Neck showing yaw rotation for tusk swiping

Highlight where front legs attach to shoulder vs back legs to hip

Label "Z up, +Y forward" axis indicator in corner

Color-code bones: spine chain in blue, legs in green, head/jaw in red, tail in yellow


Boar proportions: short snout with tusks, broad chest, mane spikes along spine, short legs, small curled tail. Realistic-stylized, like Palworld or Genshin Impact aesthetic. White background, clean technical

illustration style.

comments.author: Capital-Meringue-168
comments.body:
The biggest win for me on non humanoid rigs has been getting AI to draft an initial bone hierarchy and naming convention before I open Blender. I throw in 2-3 anatomy references, ask it where the joints should go, and tweak the output by hand.



Where it falls apart is asymmetric stuff, multi armed characters or weird joint counts on each side. Those still need a human to actually plan out the joint layout.
